claim: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a blood cancer characterized by dysregulated production of maturing myeloid cells driven by the product of the Philadelphia chromosome, the BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase.
source: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a blood cancer characterized by dysregulated production of maturing myeloid cells driven by the product of the Philadelphia chromosome, the BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CML and is stated as a defining characteristic in the abstract.

claim: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have proved effective in treating CML.
source: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have proved effective in treating CML, but there is still a cohort of patients who do not respond to TKI therapy even in the absence of mutations in the BCR-ABL1 kinase domain that mediate drug resistance.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about TKI effectiveness in CML treatment.

claim: There is a cohort of CML patients who do not respond to TKI therapy even in the absence of BCR-ABL1 kinase domain mutations that mediate drug resistance.
source: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have proved effective in treating CML, but there is still a cohort of patients who do not respond to TKI therapy even in the absence of mutations in the BCR-ABL1 kinase domain that mediate drug resistance.
evidence: This is a known clinical observation cited as motivation for the study.

claim: A nonlinear mathematical model of CML hematopoiesis was developed that incorporates feedback control and lineage branching.
source: To discover novel strategies to improve TKI therapy in CML, we developed a nonlinear mathematical model of CML hematopoiesis that incorporates feedback control and lineage branching.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study describing the model development.

claim: Cell–cell interactions were constrained using an automated model selection method together with previous observations and new in vivo data from a chimeric BCR-ABL1 transgenic mouse model of CML.
source: Cell–cell interactions were constrained using an automated model selection method together with previous observations and new in vivo data from a chimeric BCR-ABL1 transgenic mouse model of CML.
evidence: This describes the methodology used to develop and constrain the model.

claim: The quantitative model captures the dynamics of normal and CML cells at various stages of the disease and exhibits variable responses to TKI treatment, consistent with those of CML patients.
source: The resulting quantitative model captures the dynamics of normal and CML cells at various stages of the disease and exhibits variable responses to TKI treatment, consistent with those of CML patients.
evidence: This is a primary finding describing the model's capabilities and validation.

claim: The model predicts that an increase in the proportion of CML stem cells in the bone marrow would decrease the tendency of the disease to respond to TKI therapy.
source: The model predicts that an increase in the proportion of CML stem cells in the bone marrow would decrease the tendency of the disease to respond to TKI therapy, in concordance with clinical data and confirmed experimentally in mice.
evidence: This is a model prediction that is supported by both clinical data and experimental validation in mice.

claim: The model prediction that increased CML stem cell proportion decreases TKI response is in concordance with clinical data and confirmed experimentally in mice.
source: The model predicts that an increase in the proportion of CML stem cells in the bone marrow would decrease the tendency of the disease to respond to TKI therapy, in concordance with clinical data and confirmed experimentally in mice.
evidence: This describes validation of the model prediction through both clinical data and experimental evidence.

claim: Under assumed similarities between normal and leukemic cells, a key predictor of refractory response to TKI treatment is an increased maximum probability of self-renewal of normal hematopoietic stem cells.
source: The model further suggests that, under our assumed similarities between normal and leukemic cells, a key predictor of refractory response to TKI treatment is an increased maximum probability of self-renewal of normal hematopoietic stem cells.
evidence: This is a model prediction based on the assumptions and structure of the mathematical model.

claim: The model predicts that stimulating the differentiation of leukemic stem cells while applying TKI therapy can significantly improve treatment outcomes.
source: The model predicts that stimulating the differentiation of leukemic stem cells while applying TKI therapy can significantly improve treatment outcomes.
evidence: This is a therapeutic prediction derived from the model simulations.

claim: The hematopoietic system normally produces billions of mature myeloid and erythroid cells on a daily basis.
source: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm of the hematopoietic system, which normally produces billions of mature myeloid and erythroid cells on a daily basis, is tightly regulated, and accommodates massive increases in the production of individual cell types in response to physiological and pathological stresses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about normal hematopoiesis.

claim: The hematopoietic system is organized hierarchically as a collection of progressively more differentiated cells starting from a hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) located in the bone marrow and ending with postmitotic terminally differentiated myeloid and lymphoid cells.
source: The hematopoietic system is organized hierarchically as a collection of progressively more differentiated cells starting from a hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) located in the bone marrow (BM) and ending with postmitotic terminally differentiated myeloid and lymphoid cells (Rieger and Schroeder, 2012; Liggett and Sankaran, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about hematopoietic organization, supported by citations.

claim: CML is characterized by an overproduction of myeloid cells including mature granulocytes and their immediate precursors, and of myeloid progenitors.
source: CML is characterized by an overproduction of myeloid cells including mature granulocytes (neutrophils, basophils, and eosinophils) and their immediate precursors (metamyelocytes, myelocytes, and promyelocytes), and of myeloid progenitors (Jamieson et al., 2004) including multipotential progenitors (MPPs) and committed progenitors (common myeloid progenitors [CMP], granulocyte-macrophage progenitors [GMPs], and megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitors [MEPs]).
evidence: This is a known characteristic of CML supported by citation.

claim: Untreated CML has three distinct phases.
source: Untreated, the disease has three distinct phases (Chereda and Melo, 2015).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about CML progression, supported by citation.

claim: In the initial chronic phase of CML, the differentiation of myeloid progenitors is essentially normal, resulting in excessive levels of mature postmitotic neutrophils and their immediate precursors.
source: In the initial 'chronic' phase, the differentiation of myeloid progenitors is essentially normal, resulting in excessive levels of mature postmitotic neutrophils and their immediate precursors.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of chronic phase CML based on established knowledge.

claim: In later stages of CML (accelerated phase and blast crisis), differentiation is reduced and expansion of immature progenitors is observed.
source: In later stages of the disease (accelerated phase and blast crisis), differentiation is reduced and expansion of immature progenitors is observed.
evidence: This describes characteristics of advanced CML phases based on established knowledge.

claim: Additional clonal karyotypic abnormalities are typically only observed during the accelerated and blast crisis phases of CML.
source: Additional clonal karyotypic abnormalities are typically only observed during the accelerated and blast crisis phases (Hehlmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about CML progression, supported by citation.

claim: CML has one of the simplest cancer genomes.
source: CML has one of the simplest cancer genomes.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of CML compared to other cancers.

claim: CML is driven by a single genetic abnormality arising somatically in an HSC, the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome, the result of a balanced translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 that creates a fusion of the genes for BCR and ABL1.
source: It is driven by a single genetic abnormality arising somatically in an HSC, the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome, the result of a balanced translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 that creates a fusion of the genes for BCR and ABL1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the genetic basis of CML.

claim: The product of the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene is a dysregulated cytoplasmic protein-tyrosine kinase, BCR-ABL1.
source: The product of the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene is a dysregulated cytoplasmic protein-tyrosine kinase, BCR-ABL1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the BCR-ABL1 fusion protein.

claim: CML represents a natural model of dysregulated granulocytopoiesis.
source: CML thus represents a natural model of dysregulated granulocytopoiesis (Quintás-Cardama and Cortes, 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of CML's biological significance, supported by citation.

claim: Ph+ cells expressing markers of normal HSC are capable of engrafting immunodeficient mice.
source: Cell biological studies have shown that Ph+ cells expressing markers of normal HSC are capable of engrafting immunodeficient mice (Sirard et al., 1996; Lewis et al., 1998), implying that these cells are leukemia-initiating or leukemic 'stem' cells (LSCs).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from cited studies demonstrating LSC properties.

claim: Ph+ cells expressing HSC markers are leukemia-initiating or leukemic stem cells (LSCs).
source: Cell biological studies have shown that Ph+ cells expressing markers of normal HSC are capable of engrafting immunodeficient mice (Sirard et al., 1996; Lewis et al., 1998), implying that these cells are leukemia-initiating or leukemic 'stem' cells (LSCs).
evidence: This is an inference based on the engraftment capability demonstrated in cited studies.

claim: More mature committed progenitors in CML, like normal progenitors, lack sustained self-renewal capacity and cannot stably engraft immunodeficient mice nor generate hematopoietic colonies in vitro upon serial replating.
source: More mature committed progenitors in CML, like normal progenitors, lack sustained self-renewal capacity and cannot stably engraft immunodeficient mice nor generate hematopoietic colonies in vitro upon serial replating (Huntly et al., 2004).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from a cited study about progenitor cell properties.

claim: The proportion of LSCs in the BM is highly variable across CML patients at diagnosis and can range from a few percent to nearly 100%.
source: The proportion of LSCs in the BM is highly variable across CML patients at diagnosis and can range from a few percent to nearly 100% (Petzer et al., 1996; Diaz-Blanco et al., 2007; Abe et al., 2008; Thielen et al., 2016), perhaps reflecting different periods of time patients spend in chronic phase before they are diagnosed, different rates of disease progression, or both.
evidence: This is clinical observation from multiple cited studies.

claim: The variability in LSC proportion may reflect different periods of time patients spend in chronic phase before diagnosis, different rates of disease progression, or both.
source: The proportion of LSCs in the BM is highly variable across CML patients at diagnosis and can range from a few percent to nearly 100% (Petzer et al., 1996; Diaz-Blanco et al., 2007; Abe et al., 2008; Thielen et al., 2016), perhaps reflecting different periods of time patients spend in chronic phase before they are diagnosed, different rates of disease progression, or both.
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for LSC proportion variability.

claim: There is persuasive experimental evidence of significant feedback regulation of different cell compartments in the dynamics of myeloid cell production in both normal and CML hematopoiesis, including signaling between the normal and CML cells.
source: There is persuasive experimental evidence of significant feedback regulation of different cell compartments in the dynamics of myeloid cell production in both normal and CML hematopoiesis, including signaling between the normal and CML cells (Jiang et al., 1999; Devireddy et al., 2005; Vicente-Dueñas et al., 2009; Naka et al., 2010; Reynaud et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2012; Krause et al., 2013; Walenda et al., 2014; Welner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary of experimental evidence from multiple cited studies.

claim: IL-6, produced by leukemic neutrophils, blocked MPP differentiation toward a lymphoid fate in a mouse model of CML.
source: For instance, experiments in a mouse model of CML provided evidence that IL-6, produced by leukemic neutrophils, blocked MPP differentiation toward a lymphoid fate, implying feedback from the myeloid lineage onto MPPs (Reynaud et al., 2011).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from a cited study demonstrating a specific feedback mechanism.

claim: Knowledge of the details of feedback regulation in hematopoiesis is still incomplete, especially for granulopoiesis.
source: Surprisingly, our knowledge of the details of feedback regulation in hematopoiesis is still incomplete, especially for granulopoiesis, where even late-stage feedback interactions are poorly understood.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Mice lacking both G-CSF and GM-CSF maintain baseline neutrophil levels and can still increase neutrophil production in response to infection.
source: For example, two cytokines, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), can pharmacologically increase neutrophil production, but mice lacking both cytokines maintain baseline neutrophil levels and can still increase neutrophil production in response to infection (Basu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from a cited study demonstrating redundancy in neutrophil regulation.

claim: TKIs such as imatinib, dasatinib, and nilotinib, which inhibit proliferation and increase apoptosis of Ph+ cells, have dramatically lowered CML death rates.
source: In spite of this knowledge deficit, CML can be treated quite effectively using selective small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) of the BCR-ABL1 kinase. TKIs such as imatinib, dasatinib, and nilotinib, which inhibit proliferation and increase apoptosis of Ph+ cells, have dramatically lowered CML death rates (Gambacorti-Passerini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about TKI effectiveness, supported by citation.

claim: The response to TKI therapy in CML is monitored primarily by determining the level of BCR-ABL1 mRNA transcripts in peripheral blood, normalized to a control RNA and expressed as a percentage on an International Scale.
source: The response to TKI therapy in CML is monitored primarily by determining the level of BCR-ABL1 mRNA transcripts in peripheral blood, normalized to a control RNA and expressed as a percentage on an International Scale (Arora and Press, 2017).
evidence: This describes standard clinical practice for monitoring CML treatment, supported by citation.

claim: BCR-ABL1 transcript levels generally decrease exponentially in patients responding to TKI therapy resulting in at least two distinct slopes when plotted semi-logarithmically.
source: BCR-ABL1 transcript levels, an approximation of the proportion of circulating malignant cells at any given time, generally decrease exponentially in patients responding to TKI therapy resulting in at least two distinct slopes when plotted semi-logarithmically—an initial rapid decline attributed to TKI-induced killing of more mature myeloid cells, and a subsequent slower decline postulated to represent lower death rates of more primitive leukemic stem/progenitor cells (Michor et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a known pattern of TKI response in CML patients, supported by citation.

claim: The initial rapid decline in BCR-ABL1 transcripts is attributed to TKI-induced killing of more mature myeloid cells.
source: BCR-ABL1 transcript levels, an approximation of the proportion of circulating malignant cells at any given time, generally decrease exponentially in patients responding to TKI therapy resulting in at least two distinct slopes when plotted semi-logarithmically—an initial rapid decline attributed to TKI-induced killing of more mature myeloid cells, and a subsequent slower decline postulated to represent lower death rates of more primitive leukemic stem/progenitor cells (Michor et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the biphasic response pattern, supported by citation.

claim: Clinical resistance to TKI therapy in CML is a significant problem and is classified as acquired resistance or primary resistance.
source: Clinical resistance to TKI therapy in CML is a significant problem and is classified as acquired resistance (increasing BCR-ABL1 transcript levels following a substantial decrease) or primary resistance (lack of an adequate initial response).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about TKI resistance patterns.

claim: Many patients with acquired resistance have developed mutations in the BCR-ABL1 kinase domain that mediate pharmacological resistance to the TKI.
source: Many patients with acquired resistance have developed mutations in the BCR-ABL1 kinase domain that mediate pharmacological resistance to the TKI (Ernst and Hochhaus, 2012).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about acquired resistance mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: 10–15% of newly diagnosed CML patients fail to achieve an early molecular response, defined as the level of BCR-ABL1 transcripts being less than 10% at 3 months.
source: By contrast, 10–15% of newly diagnosed CML patients fail to achieve an 'early molecular response,' defined as the level of BCR-ABL1 transcripts being less than 10% at 3 mo (Hanfstein et al., 2012; Marin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is clinical data from cited studies about primary resistance rates.

claim: Clinical data indicate that switching TKIs may not benefit patients who fail to achieve early molecular response.
source: Clinical data indicate that switching TKIs may not benefit these patients (Yeung et al., 2012; Yeung et al., 2015), suggesting that this group is destined to do poorly regardless of the specific inhibitor used.
evidence: This is clinical evidence from cited studies about treatment outcomes.

claim: BCR-ABL1 mutations are generally not present in patients with primary resistance.
source: BCR-ABL1 mutations are generally not present in this group of patients (Zhang et al., 2009; Pietarinen et al., 2016), and thus the mechanism(s) underlying this primary resistance is unclear.
evidence: This is clinical observation from cited studies.

claim: The mechanism(s) underlying primary resistance in patients without BCR-ABL1 mutations is unclear.
source: BCR-ABL1 mutations are generally not present in this group of patients (Zhang et al., 2009; Pietarinen et al., 2016), and thus the mechanism(s) underlying this primary resistance is unclear.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge about primary resistance mechanisms.

claim: Variable patient responses to TKI therapy arise from nonlinearity introduced by non-cell-autonomous interactions between normal and CML cells.
source: We hypothesized that these variable patient responses to TKI therapy arise from nonlinearity introduced by non-cell-autonomous interactions between normal and CML cells.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study that motivated the model development.

claim: Design Space Analysis (DSA) reduced the potential model space from about 60,000 models to a single model class.
source: This approach allows us to reduce the potential model space from about 60,000 models to a single model class and reveals the existence of feedforward and feedback mechanisms.
evidence: This describes the result of applying DSA to model selection.

claim: The model selection approach reveals the existence of feedforward and feedback mechanisms.
source: This approach allows us to reduce the potential model space from about 60,000 models to a single model class and reveals the existence of feedforward and feedback mechanisms.
evidence: This is a finding from the model selection process.

claim: Assuming positive or negative regulation of self-renewal and differentiation probabilities and division rates of any cell type from any other cell type results in 59,049 models.
source: Assuming that there is either positive or negative regulation of the self-renewal and differentiation probabilities and division rates of any cell type from any other cell type results in 59,049 models, counting each combination of regulated signaling as a separate model.
evidence: This is a calculation of the combinatorial complexity of possible model architectures.

claim: Using Design Space Analysis, four candidate model classes were identified that differ in how HSCs are regulated.
source: Using Design Space Analysis, four candidate model classes are identified that differ in how HSCs are regulated.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and described in the text as a result of DSA.

claim: The four model classes require negative regulation of the stem cell self-renewal fraction.
source: The result of this procedure is the elimination of all but the four model classes shown in Figure 1B, which require negative regulation of the stem cell self-renewal fraction but differ by where this regulation arises.
evidence: This is a finding from the DSA analysis describing a common feature of viable models.

claim: IL-6 is produced by differentiated myeloid cells and acts to bias MPPs toward a myeloid fate.
source: Interleukin-6 (IL-6) is produced by differentiated myeloid cells and acts to bias MPPs toward a myeloid fate (Reynaud et al., 2011; Welner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from cited studies about IL-6 function.

claim: Negative feedback circuits known as fate control provide an effective strategy for robust control of cell proliferation and reduction of oscillations in branched lineages.
source: Such negative feedback circuits, known as fate control, have been shown to provide an effective strategy for robust control of cell proliferation and reduction of oscillations in branched lineages (Buzi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is theoretical knowledge from a cited study about feedback control mechanisms.

claim: CCL3 (MIP-1α) is produced in BM by basophilic myeloid progenitors.
source: The chemokine CCL3 (also known as macrophage inhibitory protein α [MIP-1α]), produced in BM by basophilic myeloid progenitors (Baba et al., 2016), acts to inhibit the proliferation and self-renewal of normal HSC (Broxmeyer et al., 1989; Staversky et al., 2018), but CML HSC are relatively resistant to its action (Eaves et al., 1993, Baba et al., 2013).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from cited studies about CCL3 production.

claim: CCL3 acts to inhibit the proliferation and self-renewal of normal HSC.
source: The chemokine CCL3 (also known as macrophage inhibitory protein α [MIP-1α]), produced in BM by basophilic myeloid progenitors (Baba et al., 2016), acts to inhibit the proliferation and self-renewal of normal HSC (Broxmeyer et al., 1989; Staversky et al., 2018), but CML HSC are relatively resistant to its action (Eaves et al., 1993, Baba et al., 2013).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from cited studies about CCL3 function.

claim: CML HSC are relatively resistant to CCL3 action.
source: The chemokine CCL3 (also known as macrophage inhibitory protein α [MIP-1α]), produced in BM by basophilic myeloid progenitors (Baba et al., 2016), acts to inhibit the proliferation and self-renewal of normal HSC (Broxmeyer et al., 1989; Staversky et al., 2018), but CML HSC are relatively resistant to its action (Eaves et al., 1993, Baba et al., 2013).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from cited studies about differential CCL3 sensitivity.

claim: Low-dose (50 cGy) ionizing radiation is selectively toxic to HSC in the BM.
source: As described in 'Methods,' healthy C57BL6/J (B6) mice were treated with low-dose (50 cGy) ionizing radiation, previously shown to be selectively toxic to HSC in the BM (Stewart et al., 1998).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from a cited study about radiation effects on HSC.

claim: One day after 50 cGy irradiation, there was an acute approximately twofold decrease in the relative size of the HSC compartment in irradiated mice.
source: One day after treatment, we observed an acute approximately twofold decrease in the relative size of the HSC compartment in the irradiated mice (Figure 2B), accompanied by approximately threefold increase in proliferation rates for both HSC and MPPs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2B.

claim: One day after 50 cGy irradiation, there was an approximately threefold increase in proliferation rates for both HSC and MPPs.
source: One day after treatment, we observed an acute approximately twofold decrease in the relative size of the HSC compartment in the irradiated mice (Figure 2B), accompanied by approximately threefold increase in proliferation rates for both HSC and MPPs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 2C.

claim: After 50 cGy irradiation, there was no significant change in MPP population, and the system returned to equilibrium by day 7.
source: There was no significant change in MPP population, however, and the system returned to equilibrium by day 7.
evidence: This is experimental observation from the irradiation study.

claim: The HSC population exerts negative feedback on their own division rate and inhibits the division of MPPs through a negative feedforward loop.
source: These results suggest that the HSC population exerts negative feedback on their own division rate (η1) and inhibits the division of MPPs through a negative feedforward loop on η2.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results of the irradiation study.

claim: Treatment with anti-granulocyte antibody RB68C5 (50 μg) resulted in an ~20% decrease in mature BM myeloid cells.
source: B6 mice were treated with the anti-granulocyte antibody RB68C5 (50 μg), and their BM was analyzed 1 d after treatment (see 'Methods'). This treatment resulted in an ~20% decrease in mature BM myeloid cells, as measured by CD11b expression (Figure 2D and E), and was accompanied by a concomitant increase in the size of the phenotypic MPP compartment (Figure 2E) and a decrease in the HSC compartment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is experimental data from the antibody depletion study shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Myeloid cell depletion with RB68C5 was accompanied by a concomitant increase in the size of the phenotypic MPP compartment and a decrease in the HSC compartment.
source: B6 mice were treated with the anti-granulocyte antibody RB68C5 (50 μg), and their BM was analyzed 1 d after treatment (see 'Methods'). This treatment resulted in an ~20% decrease in mature BM myeloid cells, as measured by CD11b expression (Figure 2D and E), and was accompanied by a concomitant increase in the size of the phenotypic MPP compartment (Figure 2E) and a decrease in the HSC compartment (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is experimental data from the antibody depletion study shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is a negative feedback loop from the myeloid cells onto the MPP self-renewal fraction.
source: These results suggest that there is a negative feedback loop from the myeloid cells onto the MPP self-renewal fraction p1.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results of the myeloid depletion study.

claim: Out of ~10^6 possible parameter combinations, a total of 1493 parameter sets were accepted for the normal hematopoiesis model.
source: Out of ~106 possible parameter combinations, a total of 1493 parameter sets were accepted (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This describes the result of the parameter estimation procedure.

claim: Restricting to parameter sets with sufficiently large feedforward gains on the MPP division rate (γ5 > 0.01) reduced the number of eligible parameter sets to 563.
source: We further restricted the candidate parameter sets by considering only those with sufficiently large feedforward gains on the MPP division rate (γ5 > 0.01) in order to focus on the novel feedforward dynamics. This reduced the number of eligible parameter sets to 563, and their distributions are shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.
evidence: This describes a filtering step in the parameter selection process.

claim: Each accepted parameter set can be thought of as representing the 'normal' condition of a virtual patient with person-to-person variability.
source: Each of these parameter sets can be thought of as representing the 'normal' condition of a virtual patient by having different individual parameters, for example, due to genetic, epigenetic or environment factors, that nevertheless result in a 'normal' homeostatic hematopoietic system.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the parameter sets represent in the modeling framework.

claim: The different parameter sets model a range of variability across individual CML patients.
source: The different parameter sets thus model a range of variability across individual CML patients.
evidence: This is an interpretation of how the parameter sets relate to patient variability.

claim: DSA identifies four regions in the γ1 and γ3 plane in which the dynamics are governed by different S-systems.
source: As indicated in Figure 3A, DSA identifies four regions (design space) in the γ1 and γ3 plane which the dynamics are governed by different S-systems.
evidence: This is a result of applying DSA to analyze parameter sensitivity, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The dynamics in design space regions i and ii are monotonic while those in regions iii and iv are not.
source: The dynamics in regions i and ii are monotonic while those in regions iii and iv are not (e.g., the equilibria in regions i and ii are stable nodes, while those in regions iii and iv are stable spirals).
evidence: This is an analysis of the dynamic behavior in different design space regions.

claim: The equilibrium cell populations in design space region iii correspond more closely to the physiological populations identified by Manesso et al., 2013.
source: The equilibrium cell populations in region iii correspond more closely to the physiological populations identified by Manesso et al., 2013.
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions with literature values.

claim: The model robustly returns to steady state following perturbations of myeloid cells over times consistent with previous experiments.
source: While the presence of the negative feedback loops introduces small magnitude oscillations of the HSC, MPPs, and lymphoid cells, the myeloid cell dynamics are monotonic and the system robustly returns to its steady state over times that are consistent with those established in previous experiments (Reynaud et al., 2011) for similar perturbation studies.
evidence: This is a model prediction validated against experimental timescales from cited work.

claim: The only difference between normal and leukemic lineages in the initial model is a decrease in the feedback strength for leukemic HSC.
source: In particular, the model for normal and CML cells shares the same lineage structure and feedback architecture with both normal and mutant cell types providing a source of regulating factors, and although all the leukemic parameters (Appendix 1—table 3) could be different from their normal counterparts (Appendix 1—table 2), we begin by assuming the only difference between the two lineages is a decrease in the feedback strength for leukemic HSC (HSCL; SL), as indicated by p0L in the schematic in Figure 4A.
evidence: This describes a key modeling assumption about the difference between normal and CML cells.

claim: Making leukemic cells less responsive to negative feedback enables leukemic cells to gain a competitive advantage for growth.
source: This makes the leukemic cells less responsive to negative feedback and enables leukemic cells to gain a competitive advantage for growth.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequence of the modeling assumption.

claim: After introduction of a few HSCL at equilibrium of the normal hematopoietic system, the CML cells repopulate the BM at the expense of normal cells.
source: An example of CML hematopoiesis is shown in Figure 4B, where it is seen that, after the introduction of a few HSCL at equilibrium of the normal hematopoietic system, the CML cells (dashed curves) repopulate the BM at the expense of normal cells (solid curves).
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Because of negative feedback, the system will eventually reach a new equilibrium consisting solely of leukemic cells in the absence of treatment.
source: Because of negative feedback, the system will eventually reach a new equilibrium consisting solely of leukemic cells.
evidence: This is a model prediction about the long-term behavior without treatment.

claim: The model results are insensitive to changes in the other leukemic cell parameters.
source: The results are insensitive to changes in the other leukemic cell parameters (see Appendix 1, Section 9, Figure 6—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: This is a result of parameter sensitivity analysis.

claim: CML long-term culture initiating cells (LTC-IC) decrease significantly in in vitro cultures while the number of normal LTC-IC is unchanged, consistent with a relative decrease in self-renewal probability of the CML cells.
source: For example, CML long-term culture initiating cells (LTC-IC; thought to be phenotypically similar to stem cells) decrease significantly in in vitro cultures while the number of normal LTC-IC is unchanged, consistent with a relative decrease in self-renewal probability of the CML cells (Udomsakdi et al., 1992).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from a cited study about CML stem cell self-renewal.

claim: CML HSC engraft immunodeficient mice variably and inefficiently compared to normal human HSC.
source: In vivo, HSC self-renewal can be assessed directly through transplantation studies. In this regard, CML HSC engraft immunodeficient mice variably and inefficiently compared to normal human HSC (Wang et al., 1998) while HSC from BCR-ABL1 transgenic mice exhibit an engraftment defect upon secondary transplantation into syngeneic recipients (Schemionek et al., 2010).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from cited studies about CML HSC engraftment.

claim: HSC from BCR-ABL1 transgenic mice exhibit an engraftment defect upon secondary transplantation into syngeneic recipients.
source: In vivo, HSC self-renewal can be assessed directly through transplantation studies. In this regard, CML HSC engraft immunodeficient mice variably and inefficiently compared to normal human HSC (Wang et al., 1998) while HSC from BCR-ABL1 transgenic mice exhibit an engraftment defect upon secondary transplantation into syngeneic recipients (Schemionek et al., 2010).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from a cited study about BCR-ABL1 transgenic mouse HSC.

claim: Both engraftment results are suggestive of a relative decrease in self-renewal capacity of BCR-ABL1+ stem cells.
source: Both results are suggestive of a relative decrease in self-renewal capacity of BCR-ABL1+ stem cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental evidence about engraftment.

claim: The larger the relative fitness of leukemic cells, the more likely that CML will take over the system and dominate hematopoiesis.
source: As expected, the larger the relative fitness, the more likely that CML will take over the system and dominate hematopoiesis.
evidence: This is a model prediction about the relationship between fitness and CML progression.

claim: Transplantation of HSCL enables engraftment and myeloid cell production that leads to CML in mice.
source: In this experiment, either HSCL or leukemic MPPs (MPPL) were implanted into sublethally irradiated mice (Figure 5A). Transplantation of HSCL enables engraftment and myeloid cell production that leads to CML.
evidence: This is experimental evidence from a cited study (Reynaud et al., 2011) being modeled.

claim: Transplanting MPPLs does not allow for long-term engraftment but results in a larger fraction of donor-derived lymphoid cells after 35 days.
source: On the other hand, transplanting MPPLs does not allow for long-term engraftment but results in a larger fraction of donor-derived lymphoid cells after 35 d (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from a cited study (Reynaud et al., 2011) being modeled.

claim: IL-6 produced by differentiated myeloid cells reprograms MPPL progenitors toward a myeloid fate.
source: This study presented evidence that IL-6 produced by differentiated myeloid cells reprograms these MPPL progenitors toward a myeloid fate (Reynaud et al., 2011).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from a cited study about IL-6 function.

claim: 85 parameter sets were discarded based on inconsistency with transplant experiment results, leaving a total of 478 parameter sets remaining.
source: We then discarded those parameter sets that did not yield results consistent with a simple majority of myeloid cells for HSCL transplant and a simple majority of lymphoid cells for MPPL transplant (Reynaud et al., 2011). In particular, 85 parameter sets were discarded, leaving a total of 478 parameter sets remaining.
evidence: This describes the result of model validation against experimental data.

claim: When HSCL are transplanted, there is a larger fraction of donor-derived myeloid cells than lymphoid cells after 30 days, consistent with experiments.
source: When HSCL are transplanted (solid curves), the donor-derived MPPL (Figure 5C, left) rapidly increased as did the terminally differentiated myeloid and lymphoid cells (Figure 5C, right). Consistent with the experiments, there is a larger fraction of donor-derived myeloid cells than lymphoid cells after 30 d (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a model prediction that matches experimental observations.

claim: When MPPL are introduced, their population decreases because the MPPL do not stably engraft.
source: In contrast, when MPPL are introduced (dashed curves), their population decreases (Figure 5C, right) because the MPPL do not stably engraft.
evidence: This is a model prediction explaining the experimental observation.

claim: When MPPL are transplanted, there is a larger fraction of donor-derived lymphoid cells after 30 days because lymphoid cells are longer-lived than myeloid cells.
source: In both cases, because the MPPLs do not stably engraft and instead differentiate into lymphoid and myeloid cells, we observe that there is a larger fraction of donor-derived lymphoid cells after 30 d (Figure 5D), consistent with the experiments. This occurs because there is a decreasing flux of differentiating cells since there is no stable engraftment and the lymphoid cells are longer-lived (smaller death rate) than the shorter-lived myeloid cells, which have a larger death rate.
evidence: This is a model prediction with mechanistic explanation that matches experimental observations.

claim: The proportion of HSCL in the BM can vary widely across newly diagnosed CML patients from a few percent to nearly 100%.
source: While the overall size of the phenotypic HSC compartment is not increased in CML patients (Jamieson et al., 2004), the proportion of HSCL in the BM can vary widely across newly diagnosed CML patients from a few percent to nearly 100% (Petzer et al., 1996; Diaz-Blanco et al., 2007; Abe et al., 2008; Thielen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is clinical observation from multiple cited studies.

claim: TKI treatment was simulated by introducing a death rate of HSCL and MPPL proportional to their proliferation rates.
source: TKI treatment was initiated at three different times to achieve varying leukemic stem cell load (6, 18, and 36 mo) and was simulated by introducing a death rate of HSCL and MPPL proportional to their proliferation rates, with the HSCL proliferation rate lower than that of normal HSC (Jørgensen et al., 2006).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach for TKI treatment, with citation supporting the proliferation rate assumption.

claim: Long-term TKI therapy can decrement the CML stem cell compartment, at least in some patients.
source: While some studies have shown that primitive CML stem/progenitor cells are relatively resistant to killing by TKIs in vitro (Graham et al., 2002; Corbin et al., 2011), clinical studies suggest that long-term TKI therapy can decrement the CML stem cell compartment, at least in some patients (Etienne et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019), consistent with mathematical modeling of patient BCR-ABL1 transcript data (Tang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is clinical evidence from cited studies about TKI effects on stem cells.

claim: TKIs possess a measure of leukemia stem cell killing ability.
source: This supports the concept that TKIs possess a measure of leukemia stem cell killing ability, and we therefore included this effect in our model.
evidence: This is an inference from clinical and modeling studies used to justify a modeling choice.

claim: At early treatment time with lower (<90%) initial HSCL fractions, the numbers of MPPL and leukemic terminally differentiated cells decrease rapidly at the early stages of treatment.
source: At an early treatment time with lower (<90%) initial HSCL fractions (HSCL, Figure 6A), the numbers of MPPL (blue-dashed), leukemic terminally differentiated lymphoid (light-green-dashed), and myeloid (dark-green-dashed) decrease rapidly at the early stages of treatment and are accompanied by a rapid increase in HSCL due to the loss of negative feedback from the MPPL.
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The rapid decrease in leukemic cells at early treatment is accompanied by a rapid increase in HSCL due to the loss of negative feedback from the MPPL.
source: At an early treatment time with lower (<90%) initial HSCL fractions (HSCL, Figure 6A), the numbers of MPPL (blue-dashed), leukemic terminally differentiated lymphoid (light-green-dashed), and myeloid (dark-green-dashed) decrease rapidly at the early stages of treatment and are accompanied by a rapid increase in HSCL due to the loss of negative feedback from the MPPL.
evidence: This is a model prediction with mechanistic explanation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The simulated molecular response from early treatment compares well with clinical data measuring treatment responses to imatinib and dasatinib.
source: The simulated results compare well with clinical data from the DAISISON study of imatinib versus dasatinib in patients with newly diagnosed CML (Cortes et al., 2016) where the data corresponds to mean BCR-ABL1 transcripts, with standard deviations, adapted from Glauche et al., 2018 for patients who received imatinib (blue) or dasatinib (red).
evidence: This is validation of model predictions against clinical data from cited studies.

claim: The simulated molecular responses from intermediate and late treatment times are indicative of primary resistance.
source: The two other curves in Figure 6D correspond to the treatment times from Figure 6B (solid orange) and C (dashed orange). In these cases, the BCR-ABL1 transcripts do not decrease below the MR3 threshold, indicating that neither of these virtual patients responds adequately to TKI therapy.
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The model behaviors of partial response and no response are consistent with those observed in CML patients with primary resistance to TKI therapy.
source: These behaviors are consistent with those observed in CML patients with primary resistance to TKI therapy (Zhang et al., 2009; Yeung et al., 2012; Pietarinen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is validation of model predictions against clinical observations from cited studies.

claim: The fundamental difference between the three virtual patients is the number of leukemic stem cells at the start of therapy.
source: The fundamental difference between these three virtual patients is the number of leukemic stem cells at the start of therapy, which occurs because treatment is initiated at different times following the development of CML (early—6 mo after CML initiation ~93% initial HSCL fraction, intermediate—18 mo after CML initiation ~99% initial HSCL fraction, late—36 mo after CML initiation ~99.99% initial HSCL fraction).
evidence: This is an explanation of the modeling setup for the three scenarios.

claim: The higher the HSCL fraction at the start of therapy, the less effective the therapy.
source: Our results suggest that the higher the HSCL fraction at the start of therapy, the less effective the therapy.
evidence: This is a model prediction about the relationship between HSCL burden and treatment efficacy.

claim: Increased numbers of HSC and HSCL decrease their own proliferation rates as well as those of the MPPs and MPPL through feedback/feedforward regulation.
source: This follows from the feedback/feedforward regulation where increased numbers of HSC and HSCL decrease their own proliferation rates as well as those of the MPPs and MPPL (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Appendix 1—figure 6 for further explorations of feedback/feedforward regulation of parameters).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model structure.

claim: Reduced proliferation rates decrease the effectiveness of TKI therapy as evidence suggests TKIs preferentially target dividing leukemic cells.
source: This reduces the effectiveness of TKI therapy as evidence suggests TKIs preferentially target dividing leukemic cells (Graham et al., 2002; Corbin et al., 2011) and suggests a mechanism why some patients are destined to do poorly with TKI therapy.
evidence: This is an inference combining model predictions with experimental evidence from cited studies.

claim: Mice bearing smaller populations of HSCL showed a decrease in the percentage of circulating BCR-ABL1+ granulocytes in response to TKI therapy.
source: By contrast and consistent with the predictions of the quantitative model, while mice bearing smaller populations of HSCL showed a decrease in the percentage of circulating BCR-ABL1+ granulocytes in response to TKI therapy, mice with the highest HSCL burden showed virtually no decrease in circulating leukemic cells (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is experimental data from the chimeric mouse study shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Mice with the highest HSCL burden showed virtually no decrease in circulating leukemic cells in response to TKI therapy.
source: By contrast and consistent with the predictions of the quantitative model, while mice bearing smaller populations of HSCL showed a decrease in the percentage of circulating BCR-ABL1+ granulocytes in response to TKI therapy, mice with the highest HSCL burden showed virtually no decrease in circulating leukemic cells (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is experimental data from the chimeric mouse study shown in Figure 6G.

claim: TKI therapy is unable to decrement the HSCL compartment in mice with predominantly BCR-ABL1+ HSC at the start of treatment.
source: Because the level of circulating granulocytes reflects the proportion of BM HSC (Wright et al., 2001; data not shown), these results demonstrate that TKI therapy is unable to decrement the HSCL compartment in mice with predominantly BCR-ABL1+ HSC at the start of treatment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results with supporting citation.

claim: Analyses of clinical data show that patients with lower leukemic stem cell burden are more likely to respond to TKI treatment.
source: While analyses of clinical data also show that patients with lower leukemic stem cell burden are more likely to respond to TKI treatment (Thielen et al., 2016), some patients with a high percentages of leukemic stem cells at the start of treatment are nonetheless still capable of responding to TKI therapy (e.g., see Figure 3 in Thielen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is clinical evidence from a cited study.

claim: Some patients with high percentages of leukemic stem cells at the start of treatment are nonetheless still capable of responding to TKI therapy.
source: While analyses of clinical data also show that patients with lower leukemic stem cell burden are more likely to respond to TKI treatment (Thielen et al., 2016), some patients with a high percentages of leukemic stem cells at the start of treatment are nonetheless still capable of responding to TKI therapy (e.g., see Figure 3 in Thielen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is clinical evidence from a cited study.

claim: Leukemic stem cell burden alone does not predict the molecular response to TKIs.
source: This suggests that leukemic stem cell burden alone does not predict the molecular response to TKIs.
evidence: This is an inference from clinical data showing variability in response.

claim: The model outcomes bear a striking resemblance to the clinical data of Thielen et al., 2016.
source: In Figure 7A, we present the results using only one choice of leukemic parameters (see Appendix 1—table 5). Other choices of leukemic parameters give similar results (see Appendix 1—figure 13). The model outcomes bear a striking resemblance to the clinical data of Thielen et al., 2016.
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions with clinical data from a cited study.

claim: Larger values of p0,max and γ1 are correlated with a decreased response to TKI therapy after leukemia develops.
source: In particular, larger values of p0,max and γ1 are correlated with a decreased response to TKI therapy after leukemia develops.
evidence: This is a model prediction from parameter distribution analysis.

claim: The effective p0L for nonresponders is larger after TKI therapy is applied than for responders.
source: In Figure 7C, we show that the effective p0L (the fraction of HSCL self-renewal after feedback) for nonresponders (orange) is larger after TKI therapy is applied than for responders (blue).
evidence: This is a model prediction shown in Figure 7C comparing responders and nonresponders.

claim: When the maximum self-renewal p0,max is larger, the leukemic stem cells experience an acute increase in self-renewal during TKI treatment, resulting in their dominance over normal stem cells that leads to decreased response to TKIs.
source: In particular, as TKI treatment kills the leukemic progenitors, this increases the effective self-renewal fraction for both normal and leukemic stem cells because of the release of negative feedback. When the maximum self-renewal p0,max is larger, the leukemic stem cells experience an acute increase in self-renewal, resulting in their dominance over normal stem cells that then leads to a decreased response to TKIs.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model of how p0,max affects treatment response.

claim: Patients with clonal hematopoiesis frequently have mutations in genes such as TET2, DNMT3A, and ASXL1 that are known to increase stem cell self-renewal.
source: Clinical data provide support for this mechanism of resistance. Patients with clonal hematopoiesis, in which there is a dominant clone driving hematopoiesis, exhibit predominantly normal hematopoiesis but frequently have mutations in the genes, such as TET2, DNMT3A, and ASXL1, that are known to increase stem cell self-renewal (Steensma, 2018).
evidence: This is clinical knowledge from a cited study about clonal hematopoiesis.

claim: CML patients whose blood cells have mutations in TET2 and ASXL1 frequently exhibit a poor response to TKI therapy.
source: Clinical data shows that CML patients whose blood cells have mutations in TET2 and ASXL1, some of which may exist prior to development of CML, frequently exhibit a poor response to TKI therapy (Kim et al., 2017; Marum et al., 2017).
evidence: This is clinical evidence from cited studies supporting the model predictions.

claim: Patients with higher stem cell self-renewal fare worse when their CML is treated using TKIs than patients with lower stem cell self-renewal.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that patients with higher stem cell self-renewal fare worse when their CML is treated using TKIs than patients with lower stem cell self-renewal.
evidence: This is an inference from clinical data and model predictions.

claim: All the prognostic tests achieved a more accurate prediction of patient outcome using the 3–6-month data compared to the same test applied to the first 3 months.
source: All the prognostic tests achieved a more accurate prediction of patient outcome using the 3–6-month data compared to the same test applied to the first 3 mo (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a result of testing prognostic criteria on patient data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The results suggest that the prognostic criteria based on relative change may perform better than the EMR and velocity-based prognostics in the 3–6-month time frame.
source: Although the number of patients was small, the results suggest that our prognostic criteria may perform better than the EMR and velocity-based prognostics that are in current clinical use.
evidence: This is an inference from limited patient data analysis.

claim: The proportion of parameter sets that achieve MR3 under combined TKI and differentiation therapy depends nonmonotonically on the strength Δ of the differentiation therapy, with peak response (86.8%) occurring at Δ = 0.24.
source: As differentiation therapy strength increases from zero, the proportion of parameter sets that achieve MR3 increases before leveling off between Δ = 0.2–0.3, with maximum efficacy occurring at a strength of differentiation Δ of about 0.24.
evidence: This is a model prediction from testing combination therapy shown in Figure 8A.

claim: With too great a strength of differentiation treatment, the combination therapy becomes inferior to TKI therapy alone.
source: The efficacy of combination therapy then begins to decline rapidly, and with too great a strength of differentiation treatment, the combination therapy becomes inferior to TKI therapy alone.
evidence: This is a model prediction about the limits of combination therapy efficacy.

claim: Differentiation promoters allow nonresponders to TKI therapy with large self-renewal fractions to reach MR3.
source: Differentiation promoters allow nonresponders to TKI therapy with large self-renewal fractions to reach MR3.
evidence: This is a model prediction about the benefit of combination therapy for specific patient types.

claim: Loss of MR3 in a TKI responder under combination therapy primarily occurs only at the smallest self-renewal fractions.
source: The opposite outcome, loss of MR3 in a TKI responder, primarily occurs only at the smallest self-renewal fractions.
evidence: This is a model prediction about when combination therapy may be detrimental.

claim: The differentiation promoter attenuates the rapid increases in the rates of change at early times after therapy starts in both normal and leukemic cells, but the attenuation is much larger in the leukemic cells.
source: The differentiation promoter attenuates the rapid increases in the rates of change at early times after therapy starts in both normal and leukemic cells, but the attenuation is much larger in the leukemic cells.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model of how differentiation therapy works.

claim: For large values of HSC self-renewal and corresponding feedback gains, the differentiation promoter acts to bring the self-renewal fraction of the normal HSC closer to that of the HSCL, which enables the TKI therapy to disadvantage the leukemic cells.
source: Effectively, for large values of HSC self-renewal and corresponding feedback gains, the differentiation promoter acts to bring the self-renewal fraction of the normal HSC closer to that of the HSCL, which then enables the TKI therapy to disadvantage the leukemic cells, and allow for repopulation and dominance by normal cells.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation from the model of how combination therapy overcomes resistance.
